transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I keep forgetting everyday things—appointments, errands, even important family plans—and it’s starting to cause problems at home. It's creating some tension with my husband because he feels like he can't rely on me for family logistics, and my usual ways of staying organized just aren't working anymore.
Do you feel that your forgetfulness is mainly because you are constantly worried or distracted, or does it seem like a true memory problem even when you are calm and trying to focus?

It definitely feels more like a distraction and focus issue rather than a deep memory problem or being worried. Even when I sit down and try to focus calmly, my mind quickly wanders off to thoughts about dinner or my garden, or I get pulled away by a noise outside. That's usually how I end up leaving things half-finished or forgetting them entirely.
Have these attention and forgetfulness problems caused a clear decline in your ability to manage work, home tasks, or daily life, or are you still able to function pretty much as usual despite them?

Yes, there has been a very clear decline, especially since I scaled back my consulting work 18 months ago and lost that external structure. I've been double-booking plans and even missed my son's school meeting, which has caused ongoing arguments with my husband because he feels he can't rely on me for family logistics. It’s definitely disrupting our daily life much more than it ever used to.

Have you also noticed any other change in thinking, such as getting lost in familiar places, trouble finding words, or difficulty with judgment and problem-solving, or is it mainly the attention and forgetfulness you described?

No, I haven't had any trouble finding words or getting lost in familiar places; it really is just the attention and forgetfulness I described. My mind just constantly wanders off or gets distracted by my surroundings, rather than me experiencing any of those other types of confusion.
Have you noticed any new problems with judgment, planning, or solving everyday problems, or is it mainly forgetfulness and distractibility without other thinking changes?

My basic judgment feels fine, but I'm having a really hard time with planning, organizing, and following through on tasks. Without my old work structure, I'll start things like mortgage paperwork or planning a trip, only to get distracted and leave them half-finished while double-booking our family schedule. So while my thinking is clear, actually executing plans is where I'm really struggling.
Have these attention and memory problems caused only mild difficulty, or have they clearly interfered with your independence in daily life, work, or managing home responsibilities?

I'm still independent and capable of doing things on my own, but these issues have definitely caused clear and frustrating interference in my daily life. Missing my son's school meetings and constantly double-booking commitments has made managing home responsibilities really difficult. It has created a lot of tension with my husband because he feels like he can't rely on me for our family logistics anymore.
Would you say these attention and memory problems are causing only mild difficulty, or are they clearly interfering with your independence in daily life and responsibilities?

I would say the difficulty is relatively mild because I'm still fully independent, but it definitely interferes with my daily responsibilities. It has caused me to miss school meetings and double-book commitments, leading to arguments with my husband because he feels he can't rely on me for family logistics.
Have these attention and memory problems been getting steadily worse over time, or have they stayed fairly stable without a clear progression?

The underlying focus struggles have actually been there since I was a child, so they've been fairly stable long-term. However, they became much more disruptive about 18 months ago when I stepped back from consulting. Without that rigid external structure, the coping strategies I used to hide these lifelong issues just stopped working.
Were these attention and organization problems present since childhood or adolescence, or did they first begin later in adulthood after a medical illness, injury, or other brain-related event?

Yes, these struggles have definitely been present since childhood, rather than starting recently from any illness or injury. Even back in elementary school, my teachers wrote on report cards that I was bright but constantly daydreaming, chatting, and forgetting to turn in homework I'd actually finished. My parents also used to joke that I was always "off in my own world" instead of doing my chores.

Would you say these lifelong attention and organization problems cause only mild trouble in your daily life, or do they clearly interfere with your ability to function independently at home, work, or in relationships?

While the overall issues might seem mild on paper because I can still manage basic daily living, they absolutely interfere with my relationships and home life. It has led to ongoing arguments with my husband because he feels he can't rely on me for family logistics, especially after I've missed school meetings and double-booked our commitments.
Did you have any head injury, stroke, seizure, or other medical/neurologic illness around the time these problems became noticeably worse 18 months ago?

No, I haven't had any head injuries, strokes, seizures, or other medical illnesses. The worsening 18 months ago was strictly because I lost the rigid structure of my consulting work, rather than any kind of medical event.
Besides the distractibility, have you also had lifelong symptoms like being very fidgety, unable to sit still, talking excessively, interrupting others, or acting impulsively?

Yes, absolutely; I constantly fidget by bouncing my leg or tapping a pen, and sitting still for over thirty minutes makes me feel so restless and "itchy" that my husband jokes I don't know how to just sit on the couch. I also have a lifelong habit of interrupting people to blurt out ideas, which ties back to my elementary school days when teachers always noted I was constantly chatting in class.
Before age 12, did these attention and restlessness symptoms cause problems at school or at home, such as frequent careless mistakes, unfinished work, or behavior comments from teachers?

Yes, they definitely caused issues back then. On my elementary school report cards, teachers often wrote that I was bright but constantly daydreaming, chatting, and forgetting to turn in homework I had actually finished. My parents also used to joke that I was always "off in my own world" instead of completing my chores.
Have these attention, restlessness, and impulsive symptoms continued into adulthood without long symptom-free periods, or did they mostly go away and then return later?

They never actually went away; they've been present since childhood and college. I managed to keep them hidden and under control for years by relying on extremely rigid schedules and meticulous lists. Once I lost that external structure eighteen months ago, the symptoms became highly visible and disruptive again.
Do you also have ongoing hyperactive or impulsive behaviors that cause problems, such as being unable to stay seated, feeling internally restless, interrupting others, or acting before thinking?

Yes, I definitely struggle with those behaviors. If I have to sit still for more than half an hour, like during Zoom calls, I get a pent-up, almost "itchy" restless feeling that leads to fidgeting like bouncing my leg, and my husband jokes I don't know how to just sit on the couch. I also frequently find myself interrupting others or blurting out ideas during family or garden planning conversations before people can even finish their sentences.
Do your fidgeting, interrupting, or restlessness cause significant problems at work, in relationships, or in other settings, or are they mostly noticeable but not very disruptive?

The fidgeting and interrupting are definitely noticeable and cause some awkwardness—like people glancing at me in meetings or feeling embarrassed when I blurt things out—but they aren't the main source of conflict. The truly disruptive problems causing tension and arguments with my husband are the forgetfulness, missed appointments, and my struggle to keep track of family logistics.
Do your fidgeting, interrupting, or feeling unable to sit still cause major problems in your daily life, or are the main problems still the inattention and forgetfulness?

The fidgeting, restlessness, and interrupting are definitely there, but they don't cause major disruptions in my life. The primary, most stressful problems causing friction at home are definitely my forgetfulness and inattention. It's the missed appointments and my struggle to keep track of family plans that really cause the tension.

Would you say your main ongoing problem is inattention and disorganization, or are hyperactive/impulsive symptoms like restlessness, interrupting, and acting before thinking equally prominent and impairing?

To be honest, both aspects are actually very prominent in my life. While the forgetfulness and disorganization are what finally pushed me to seek help, I also constantly struggle with physical restlessness, like feeling antsy if I sit still too long, and I frequently interrupt or blurt things out during family and community meetings.
Which is more prominent in your day-to-day life: inattention and disorganization, or hyperactive/impulsive symptoms like restlessness, interrupting, and acting before thinking?

Both aspects affect me heavily in my daily life. While the inattention and forgetfulness, like missing appointments and losing track of tasks, cause the most disruption and friction at home, I also constantly struggle with physical restlessness, an inability to sit still, and a tendency to blurt things out or interrupt others.
Which causes you more impairment in your daily life: trouble paying attention and staying organized, or being very restless, interrupting, or acting impulsively?

The trouble with paying attention, staying organized, and forgetting things definitely causes much more impairment in my daily life. My forgetfulness and lack of follow-through have led to missed appointments, double-bookings, and a lot of tension with my husband over family logistics. While my restlessness and tendency to interrupt are noticeable and annoying, they don't disrupt our daily household routines nearly as severely.

Before age 12, did your symptoms cause problems mainly with inattention and disorganization, or did they also clearly include significant hyperactivity or impulsive behavior that caused trouble at school or home?

It was definitely a mix of both back then. My teachers often noted on my report cards that I was bright but constantly daydreaming, chatting, and forgetting to turn in homework I had actually finished. At home, my parents always joked that I was "off in my own world" instead of actually completing my chores.
Before age 12, were your symptoms mainly inattentive and disorganized, or did you also have clear hyperactive/impulsive behaviors that caused problems at school or home?

Back in elementary school, my struggles were definitely more on the inattentive side, like daydreaming, being "off in my own world," and forgetting to turn in completed homework. I did chat a lot in class, which my teachers noted on my report cards, but it was mostly daydreaming and disorganization rather than any major physical hyperactivity.

As an adult, do you still have clear hyperactive or impulsive symptoms, such as feeling unable to sit still, fidgeting a lot, interrupting others, or acting before thinking, and do these cause problems for you?

Yes, I definitely still struggle with those behaviors as an adult. If I have to sit still for too long, I get a restless, "itchy" feeling and start fidgeting by bouncing my leg or tapping my pen, and I often interrupt others or blurt out thoughts. It makes it really hard for me to ever truly relax and causes ongoing tension with my husband.
As an adult, do your restlessness, interrupting, or impulsive behaviors cause clear problems in your daily life and relationships, or are they mostly mild and not very impairing?

Yes, they definitely cause clear problems rather than being mild. My difficulty with organizing and following through has led to missed school meetings and double-booked plans, causing ongoing arguments with my husband because he feels he can't rely on me for family logistics. I also frequently embarrass myself by interrupting and blurting things out during family conversations and community garden meetings.
Which causes you more problems day to day: trouble paying attention and staying organized, or hyperactive/impulsive symptoms like restlessness, interrupting, or acting before thinking?

I definitely experience both, but the trouble paying attention, staying organized, and forgetting things causes much more day-to-day disruption and friction. While I am quite restless and catch myself interrupting others, it is the forgotten appointments, double-bookings, and unfinished tasks that cause the real problems with my family and schedule.
Did your hyperactive or impulsive symptoms, like fidgeting, interrupting, or feeling unable to sit still, also clearly begin before age 12 and continue consistently into adulthood?

Yes, those patterns definitely go back to my childhood. My elementary school report cards often noted I was bright but constantly chatting and daydreaming, and my parents joked I was always "off in my own world." I managed to keep these traits under control as an adult by staying constantly busy with rigid schedules and lists, but they became highly disruptive again once I lost that structure eighteen months ago.

Do your hyperactive or impulsive symptoms, like fidgeting, interrupting, or feeling unable to sit still, cause clear impairment in your daily life, or are they mostly noticeable but not very disruptive?

While my fidgeting, restlessness, and interrupting are definitely noticeable and sometimes embarrassing, they aren't the main source of disruption in my life. The real impairment and friction at home come from my struggles with memory and organization, such as forgetting appointments and failing to follow through on family plans.
